power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Enumeration of circulating immune cells is an established clinical practice implemented across a plethora of indications.
While flow cytometry is the gold standard for this task, cellular deconvolution algorithms provide a robust computational alternative using molecular data.
These digital cytometry pipelines typically rely on millilitre-scale venous blood samples.

Here, we evaluated the potential of capillary blood microsampling as a patient-centric and minimally invasive approach for the digital cytometry of major lymphocyte populations (T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells; TBNK).
In a cohort of 200 participants, we compared RNA sequencing based deconvolution performance between matched PAXgene-stabilised venous blood and Mitra capillary blood microsamples.
While venous transcriptomes enabled highly accurate TBNK estimation, patient-matched capillary microsamples exhibited a significant reduction in deconvolution accuracy.
Computational adaptations, including the integration of capillary-specific single-cell reference profiles, yielded only limited improvements.
Instead, our analyses revealed that the performance deficit was primarily driven by the decreased transcriptome complexity of the capillary microsample libraries.

This study highlights the critical role of transcript diversity for cellular deconvolution and reveals the current pre-analytical challenges that must be overcome to harness transcriptomics based digital cytometry using dried blood microsamples.
The composition of circulating immune cells provides clinically valuable information for disease diagnosis, patient stratification, and longitudinal health monitoring.
Flow cytometry is commonly used to measure immune cell populations directly but requires intact cells, specialised equipment, and time-sensitive sample processing.

Digital cytometry provides a complementary computational approach in which corresponding cell type fractions are estimated from molecular measurements, including transcriptomic [1] and epigenetic data [2].

A wide range of bioinformatic methods have been developed to deconvolve bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and DNA methylation datasets into their constituent cell types.

Previous studies have demonstrated robust deconvolution of venous whole blood transcriptomes into their constituent immune cell populations, with strong correlations between computationally estimated cell fractions and flow cytometric measurements [3, 4, 5, 6, 7].

text.text: These studies have generally relied on millilitre-scale venous blood samples collected by trained personnel through venipuncture.
Capillary blood microsampling, however, typically requires 120 µL or less and offers a minimally invasive alternative that is well suited to repeated, out-of-clinic, and home-based collection [8, 9].
text.formatted: Capillary blood microsampling, however, typically requires 120 µL or less and offers a minimally invasive alternative that is well suited to repeated, out-of-clinic, and home-based collection <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Studies have shown that capillary microsamples can support reliable measurements of metabolites [10], proteins [11, 12], and drugs [13, 14] and can generate global transcriptomic profiles broadly comparable to those obtained from venous blood [15].

text.text: However, lower RNA input, differences in collection and processing, and biological differences between capillary and venous blood may affect the accuracy of transcriptome-based cell type deconvolution.

To evaluate the potential of capillary blood microsampling for digital cytometry in diagnostics and health monitoring, we investigated whether the major lymphocyte populations comprising T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells (TBNK) could be reliably deconvolved from capillary blood RNA-seq data.
We recruited 200 participants and generated paired transcriptomic profiles from capillary microsamples and venous whole blood samples.
RNA-seq-derived estimates of TBNK cell fractions were evaluated against matched flow cytometric measurements from the same participants.
This paired design allowed us to assess the accuracy of capillary blood deconvolution and compare its performance with that achieved using conventional venous samples.
The Muno-1 study was a single centre, descriptive study conducted at the rheumatology outpatient department of the Medizinicum Hamburg.
Adults aged 18 years or older without known chronic infection with HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, or anaemia, were eligible.
Recruitment continued until 200 participants had been fully enrolled.
Participants provided written informed consent before completing the study questionnaire and undergoing blood collection.
Samples and associated clinical data were pseudonymised at the study site before transfer for laboratory analysis, with the re-
The study used a paired, within-participant design.
At a single study visit, each participant underwent venous blood collection and finger-prick capillary blood microsampling.

Three matched sample modalities were generated: fresh venous whole blood for differential blood counting and flow cytometric measurement of TBNK populations; PAXgene Blood RNA Tube (BD Biosciences, catalogue no. 762165)-stabilised venous whole blood (two tubes) for RNA-seq; and dried capillary blood collected using Mitra devices with VAMS technology (Trajan Scientific, VM-304KMBD) (four 30 µL tips) for RNA-seq.
Fresh blood was collected in EDTA vacutainers and sent for same-day flow cytometry analysis at Labor Dr. von Froreich, Hamburg.

PAXgene samples were immediately frozen at -20 • C for short-term storage before transport and longer term storage at -80 • C. Mitra samples were dried and resealed in their desiccant pouch according to the manufacturer's instructions.
The samples were stored at -20 • C short-term followed by long-term storage at -80 • C until processing.
Fresh EDTA-anticoagulated venous whole blood was analysed on the day of collection at Labor Dr. von Froreich, Hamburg, using an automated AQUIOS flow-cytometry system (Beckman Coulter).
Samples were mixed immediately before loading and were processed automatically by the instrument using the AQUIOS Tetra assay.
One PAXgene Blood RNA Tube per patient was thawed overnight before total RNA extraction using QIAGEN Genomic Services' standard 96-well plate-based extraction workflow for PAXgene-stabilised blood.
RNA concentration was determined by optical-density measurement, and RNA integrity was assessed using an Agilent TapeStation and reported as the RNA integrity number equivalent (RINe).
Total RNA was extracted from two 30 µL Mitra tips using the NucleoMag RNA kit (Macherey-Nagel, 744350.4) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
The tips were dispensed into Lysis Buffer and vortexed at maximum speed for 10 s at room temperature to release RNA.
Lysates were cleared by centrifugation using Investigator Lyse & Spin Basket Kit (Qiagen, 19598) prior to further processing on a MagnetaPure 32+ automation system.
text.formatted: Lysates were cleared by centrifugation using Investigator Lyse & Spin Basket Kit <ref type="bibr">(Qiagen, 19598)</ref> prior to further processing on a MagnetaPure 32+ automation system.

text.text: RNA was eluted in 50 µL volume and quantified using Quant-iT RNA HS (ThermoFisher, Q32884).
RINe was measured using Agilent TapeStation HS RNA (Agilent, 5067-5579).
Library preparation was performed using QIAseq UPX 3' Transcriptome Kit (QIAGEN, 333088). 10 ng (PAXgene) or 1-2 ng (Mitra) purified RNA was converted into cDNA NGS libraries.
Library preparation was quality controlled using capillary electrophoresis with Agilent DNA 7500 (Agilent, 5067-1506) on a 2100 Bioanalyzer before the samples were pooled in equimolar ratios.
The library pool(s) were quantified using qPCR and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 (Illumina Inc.) sequencing instrument to an average read depth of 10 000 000 reads per sample.
Raw data was demultiplexed and FASTQ files for each pool were generated using Illumina bcl2fastq version 2.20.0.422.
Raw FASTQ reads were mapped by STARSolo version 2.7.10b [16] using default parameters and a whitelist of QIAGEN barcodes for demultiplexing.
text.formatted: Raw FASTQ reads were mapped by STARSolo version 2.7.10b <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> using default parameters and a whitelist of QIAGEN barcodes for demultiplexing.

text.text: QIAGEN barcodes were matched to their known patient IDs to generate the final count matrices.
Count matrices were imported into R 4.5.1/RStudio 2024.12.1+563 running in an Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS environment.
Principal-component Analysis (PCA) identified 1 PAXgene outlier and 4 Mitra outliers.
A further 26 Mitra samples with asymmetrical skew in the distribution of their normalised gene counts were also excluded.

With the retained 199 PAXgene and 170 Mitra samples, gene counts were normalised using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method to compute Counts Per Million (CPM) values as implemented in edgeR [17].
text.formatted: With the retained 199 PAXgene and 170 Mitra samples, gene counts were normalised using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method to compute Counts Per Million (CPM) values as implemented in edgeR <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: CIBERSORT [3], EPIC [4], and quanTIseq [5] deconvolution were performed using immunedeconv [18] R package distributed via Bioconductor version 3.19.

text.text: Ground truth (i.e., "measured") fractions of whole blood per cell type (T cells shown as an example) were computed from flow cytometry measurements as follows-T.Cells.rel(relative, %)/100 × Lymphocytes.rel(relative, %).
Custom reference profiles for EPIC deconvolution were generated from capillary blood scRNA-seq datasets [19] using the Seurat version 5.2.1 ecosystem [20].

text.text: To identify minimal gene sets capable of accurate TBNK deconvolution, a genetic algorithm-based feature selection approach was implemented.

The algorithm operated on normalised gene expression matrices (log 2 (CPM + 1) transformation) from the PAXgene datasets to identify optimal gene subsets for predicting flow-cytometry-derived TBNK fractions.
The genetic algorithm maintained a population of 500 candidate gene sets (individuals), where each individual represented a unique combination of n = 24 genes.
Initial populations were randomly seeded from the full gene expression matrix.

Fitness evaluation for each gene set employed 50-fold cross-validation using linear regression models, with fitness scores calculated as the product of Pearson correlation coefficients across TBNK predictions (Fitness = ∏ c∈{T,B,N K} r c ).
This multiplicative fitness metric ensured balanced performance across all three cell types.
Evolution proceeded through iterative generations combining selection, crossover, and mutation operations.
In each generation, the 500 fittest individuals were retained based on their fitness scores.

Breeding generated 500 offspring through weighted probabilistic selection of parent pairs (exponentially decaying probability: p i ∝ e -6i/N where i represents rank position), with each offspring inheriting genes randomly sampled from both parents.
Mutation was applied to 20 % of genes in each offspring to maintain genetic diversity.
Additionally, 250 randomly generated individuals were introduced each generation to prevent premature convergence.
To ensure robust feature selection, a leave-one-batch-out cross-validation scheme was employed.
The dataset was partitioned into 20 equal batches, with each instance of the genetic algorithm tested on a specific batch after training on the union of the remaining 19.
This process ran for 1000 generations per batch, with parallel processing across four cores to reduce computational time.
For each run, we confirmed that the fitness level within the population had plateaued for at least 50 generations prior to termination.
Final gene importance scores were calculated as the frequency of selection across all 20 independent runs, providing a consensus ranking of predictive genes for TBNK deconvolution.
The algorithm implementation utilised scikit-learn [22] version 1.5.2 for machine learning components and multiprocessing for parallelisation.

Participants in the disease group were older than those in the no-disease group, with mean ages of 46.9 and 36.6 years, respectively, and had a higher mean body mass index of 26.1 kg m -2 compared with 23.1 kg m -2 .
Women comprised the majority of both groups.
Active autoimmune disease was the most frequently recorded disease category, affecting 31.4 % of participants in the disease group.

In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using dried capillary blood microsamples for the transcriptomics-based mance in Mitra samples.

Using the same standard library preparation workflow, the dried microsamples yielded libraries with both a lower number of detected genes and a lower average read count per gene compared with stabilised venous samples.
By experimentally subsampling read counts and restricting the detectable genes in the PAXgene dataset, we were able to largely recapitulate the deterioration in TBNK fraction predictions.
This confirms the critical role of transcript diversity and abundance in successful cellular deconvolution.

However, the failure of computational downsampling to fully mirror the severity of the Mitra performance drop suggests that additional biological differences between capillary and venous blood, or other unmeasured pre-analytical variables, may also contribute to the discrepancy.
Several methodological factors inherent to our study design may account for this reduced library complexity.
The Mitra devices employ proprietary Volumetric Absorptive Microsampling (VAMS) technology, which immediately dries the postdraw blood.

While this desiccation is highly beneficial for stabilising messenger RNA at ambient temperatures and facilitating out-of-clinic or home-based sample collection [26, 27, 28], it is possible that alternative microsampling devices might preserve RNA integrity or extraction efficiency more effectively.
text.formatted: While this desiccation is highly beneficial for stabilising messenger RNA at ambient temperatures and facilitating out-of-clinic or home-based sample collection <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28]</ref>, it is possible that alternative microsampling devices might preserve RNA integrity or extraction efficiency more effectively.

text.text: Furthermore, the diminished signal in the Mitra libraries may be heavily influenced by the low input volume (2 µL) specified by the chosen library preparation protocol.
This low input likely resulted in a dilutive effect on the absolute number and diversity of transcripts captured from the total extracted RNA per sample.
Addressing these technical hurdles will be essential for the future application of digital cytometry to microsampling.
Future efforts must focus on generating capillary blood transcriptomes with a complexity on par with those derived from standard venipuncture.
Strategies to maximise library complexity could include modifying library preparation protocols to accommodate larger input volumes (e.g., ≥ 10 µL).

Additionally, employing full-length RNA-seq approaches, such as SMART-seq [29, 30], may provide a more comprehensive capture of the transcriptome than the 3'-end sequencing approach used here, potentially buffering against the low initial input mass characteristic of microsamples.

text.text: The quantification of whole blood immune cell populations remains a routine and critical task for diagnosing and monitoring disease.

While flow cytometry is the established gold standard for this purpose, its reliance on fresh tissue, complex logistics, and specialised infrastructure limits its utility in remote and high-frequency longitudinal settings.
The convergence of next-generation sequencing, bioinformatic deconvolution, and minimally invasive microsampling offers a powerful alternative.

Although our findings highlight that optimising pre-analytical processing and library complexity is a critical prerequisite, overcoming these physical sequencing limitations will ultimately unlock the potential of digital cytometry to democratise and decentralise cellular health monitoring in a digital health era.

While our experimental workflow achieved robust deconvolution of 218 TBNK fractions using stabilised venous blood (PAXgene), patient-matched dried capillary blood microsamples (Mitra) 219 exhibited a marked reduction in deconvolution accuracy.

Extensive adaptation of the reference profiles, including the 220 integration of capillary-specific single-cell marker genes and custom signatures, provided only limited cell type specific 221 improvements.
This indicated that the performance deficit could not be resolved solely through computational adjust-222 ments.
